lesson_title: The Crane, the Cats and the String
hook_text: Why does x PLUS 3 move a graph LEFT? The bracket has been answering a different question all along.
clip_script: Here's the sign that betrays everyone: y equals x plus three, all squared — and the graph moves three to the LEFT. Plus... means left? Feels broken. It isn't, and here's the fix. A parabola's lowest point lives where the squared thing equals zero. For plain x squared, that's at zero. But now the squared thing is x plus three — and x plus three hits zero at minus three. The low point didn't disobey the sign; it followed the zero. So stop reading the sign completely. Ask one question instead: what x makes the bracket zero? That x is where the graph moved. X plus three: minus three, left. X minus three: plus three, right. Never fooled again. And this one trick runs the whole topic. The hyperbola's forbidden wall stands where its bottom bracket would divide by zero. The exponential's action is anchored the same way. Three graph families, one bracket question. Add the crane — the q lifting everything — and the tension knob a, and you can read any equation like a work order: push, hoist, stretch. The graphs were never mysterious. They were just waiting for you to ask the bracket the right question.
visual_style: A glowing tent-shaped parabola sliding left as a bracket equation ticks down to zero; a wrong-way arrow crossed out; then rapid-fire: hyperbola branches curling into corners of a fence-cross, an exponential skimming its floor, all tagged with the same bracket-zero stamp.
mood: Myth-busting and empowering — a pet peeve resolved for good.
pacing: Open on the outrage, slow through the bracket-zero reveal, accelerating montage across the three families.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read every graph like a work order.
